notes: Let’s begin by defining systems operations. Systems operations involves the responsibilities tasks required to build (create), test, deploy, monitor, maintain, and safeguard complex computing systems.

The system operation activity build includes the development of reusable infrastructure templates, which are then tested, deployed, monitored, maintained, and safeguarded. The development of reusable infrastructure templates describes the create systems operations activity.

texts: Repeatable deployment of infrastructure and applications on demand.
notes: Consider automation instead of building all the pieces of a complex computing system deployment by hand. It is a best practice to use a file or application to package the description of the network and the components that will run in that network. This course will cover some of the possibilities for packaging reusable infrastructure in depth.
For the purposes of this conversation, keep in mind that varying degrees of automation can be accomplished by creating scripts, programs, or templates such as:
A Linux shell script
A Python or Ruby application
A C# application
A template format, such as AWS CloudFormation (discussed in depth in this course)

By specifying the infrastructure either declaratively or programmatically, a user can create as many deployments of it as needed, when needed.  The goal is to make the creation of the infrastructure repeatable. You can easily deploy an infrastructure you define once, into different Regions, or create development and test environments that consistently match the production environment.

texts: Key AWS services for systems operations: Network
IP ranges, routing, gateways, and security settings
*Services will be discussed in more detail later
notes: Three key areas of interest to systems operations are network, compute, and controlling access.

When a user configures a network environment in the cloud, Amazon Virtual Private Cloud (Amazon VPC) is the service used to do it. The virtual private cloud, or VPC, is the network environment into which resources will be launched, such as EC2 instances. The VPC is designed to provide greater control over the isolation of the environment and its resources from each other.

Each VPC is defined within a Region. You can have multiple VPCs in each Region, and you can have VPCs in as many Regions as you want. The subnets you define inside of a VPC can be either public or private.
rendered: *Services will be discussed in more detail

texts: Key AWS services for systems operations: Compute
IP ranges, routing, gateways, and security settings
*Services will be discussed in more detail later
notes: AWS provides a number of compute options. Amazon EC2 lets you provision virtual computing environments in the cloud. Virtually anything that can be done with a server can be done with an Amazon EC2 instance.

Most server operating systems are supported, including Windows, Red Hat, SUSE, Ubuntu, and Amazon Linux. A user can create images of the servers at any time with a few clicks or a simple API call. These images are referred to as Amazon Machine Images (AMIs), and can be reused to launch instances in the future. Amazon EC2 is highly scalable, which means that it will add more instances when needed, and terminate these instances when they are not needed. Amazon EC2 is also optimizable, as the instance types can be selected to optimize CPU, memory, storage, networking capacity, or graphics, and general purpose. Each optimized instance type comes in a variety of sizes.

texts: Key AWS services for systems operations: Access
IP ranges, routing, gateways, and security settings
*Services will be discussed in more detail later
notes: Finally, access can be managed. AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) is a service that helps a user securely control access to AWS resources for users and for programs. A user uses IAM to control who can use the AWS resources (authentication), what resources they can use and in what ways (authorization).
IAM supports granular control over access permissions, not just based on resource, but all the way down to determining which API calls for each service can be made.

Use IAM to create additional users and assign permissions to these users, following the least-privilege principle. With IAM, you can securely control access to AWS services and resources for users in an AWS account. For example, if you require administrator-level permissions, you can create an IAM user, grant that user full access, and then use those credentials to interact with AWS. Later, if there is a need to revoke or modify permissions, you can remove or modify any policies that are associated with that IAM user. Additionally, if there are multiple users that require access to an AWS account, you can create unique credentials for each user and define who has access to which resources. In other words, there is no need to share credentials. For example, you can create IAM users with read-only access to resources in an AWS account, and distribute those credentials to users that require read access.

Identity federation is another useful tool that can be used with IAM. With federation, a user can use single sign-on (SSO) to access AWS accounts using credentials from the corporate directory. Federation uses open standards, such as Security Assertion Markup Language 2.0 (SAML), to exchange identity and security information between an identity provider (IdP) and an application.

texts: Amazon Route 53 hosted zones and record sets
Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) buckets
Amazon Elastic Block Store (Amazon EBS) snapshots
Amazon Relational Database Service (Amazon RDS) database instances
notes: Some AWS service features are Regional, others are global, and others exist only in the Availability Zone in which they are created. It is important to understand the scope of the various features.

For example, when a user defines an S3 bucket, they must specify the Region where that bucket will exist. Similarly, when they capture an EC2 instance as an AMI, that AMI is available only in the Region in which it was captured. If a user wants to instantiate an instance from that AMI in a different Region, they must first copy the AMI to that other Region. AWS CloudWatch metrics, Amazon Block Store (Amazon EBS) snapshots, Amazon ElastiCache clusters, and VPCs are also all Regional. Factors that influence the selection of a region include:
Consideration of cost that vary by Region
Consideration of legal requirements that are associated with data governance
A country's laws and regulations can affect what information can cross geographical boundaries and services that are offered.
Reduce latency with geographical proximity to customers

Some resources are global. For example, when you define IAM users, groups, and roles, those resources can be referenced across all Regions in an AWS account. Hosted zones that are defined in Amazon Route 53 are also global, as are Amazon CloudFront distributions.

Some AWS service features only exist at the level of the Availability Zone. Every Region has at least two Availability Zones. For example, if a user launches an EC2 instance in the us-west-1 Region, it will be launched into an Availability Zone, such as us-west-1b. If they then want to attach a new EBS volume to that instance, they must create the volume in the same Availability Zone (us-west-1b). Otherwise, the user will not be able to attach it to that instance. Subnets and Amazon Relational Database Service (Amazon RDS) database instances are other examples of objects or constructs that are defined within an Availability Zone.

texts: Limit potential excessive charges and keep the AWS network healthy
notes: When a user creates a new AWS account, default service limits are applied. Some of these limits are soft limits. For example, if they want to run many t2.large EC2 instances in one Region as On-Demand Instances, the per-Region soft limit on those instances is 20. If they try to run a 21st instance when 20 instances are already running, they will get a capacity error. A user can create a case in the AWS Support Center and request a Service Limit Increase for their account. These requests are often approved.

There are also some hard limits. For example, The Amazon Simple Notification Service (Amazon SNS) API has a throttling feature, and it has a limit of 100 Subscribe transactions per second. Hard limits cannot be changed.
For all the details, check out the documentation page at  http://docs.aws.amazon.com/general/latest/gr/aws_service_limits.html

notes: AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) is a service that helps securely control access to AWS resources.

Use IAM to configure authentication, which is the first step, as this controls who can access AWS resources based on that authentication. IAM is not only used for user authentication. It is also used by applications and other AWS services for access.
IAM is used to configure authorization, based on knowing who the user is, is what resources users can access and what they can do to or with those resources.

IAM eliminates the need to share passwords or access keys when granting access rights to other people or systems. It also makes it easy to enable or disable a user’s access over time, and as appropriate.

Think of IAM as the tool to centrally manage access who can launch, configure, manage, and terminate the resources.  It provides granular control over access permissions, not just for people, but for systems or other applications that might make programmatic calls to other AWS resources.
Manage not just what resources can be accessed, but what action can be performed.
For example, who can terminate Amazon EC2 instances?

notes: Here is a summary of the different types of security credentials.

Every AWS account has an assigned root user through the root account. This root account has an assigned email address for the purposes of account recovery and communication. However, we recommend that you not use the root user for everyday tasks, even administrative ones. Instead, adhere to the best practice of using the root user only to create an IAM user first. Then, securely lock away the root user credentials, and use them only when needed to perform the few account and service management tasks that cannot be accomplished in other ways.

As mentioned in the previous slide, the IAM user name and password security credentials are used to access the AWS Management Console, which is also known as the console. Access keys can be used for programmatic access when they are generated for a user.
Finally, for added security, we recommend that you apply multi-factor authentication (MFA) on the root account and on any IAM users that are defined.

texts: Permission Policies | Permission Boundaries | Managed Policies | Inline Policies
notes: The four policy types, which indicate the type of permissions that are defined for the assigned users, are listed here in order of popular usage:

Identity-based policies allow a user to attach managed and inline policies to IAM identities, such as users or the groups to which users belong. A user can also attach identity-based policies to roles. Policy categories, to IAM identities that include:
Users
Groups that users belong to
Roles

Resource-based policies allow a user to attach inline policies to resources. The most common examples of resource-based policies are Amazon S3 bucket policies and IAM role trust policies. Resource-based policies are JavaScript Object Notation (JSON) policy documents.
Resource-level permissions are only available for some AWS services and resources and provide granular access control over specific objects within an AWS service.
For example, the role’s permissions policy can list specific EC2 instances and specific EBS volumes.
Resource-level permissions do not always allow all actions.
For EC2 instances, actions such as Reboot, Start, Stop, and Terminate can be specified.

Actions such as RunInstances cannot be specified, because you do not know the InstanceID before the RunInstances call is complete. Therefore, RunInstances applies to EC2 as a whole service, but not as a specific resource.
AWS Organizations service control policies (SCPs) apply permissions boundaries to AWS Organizations or organizational units (OUs).

Access control lists (ACLs) can also be used to control which principals can access a resource. ACLs are similar to resource-based policies, although they are the only policy type that does not use the JSON policy document structure. ACLs do not use the JSON policy document structure.
Remember: Policies evaluate the following logic:
Authenticate principal
Process request context:
Environment data
Resources data
Actions
Resources
Principal
Evaluate Policies based on:
Policy type
Policy category
Allow or deny request
NOTE: The evaluation order of the policies has no effect on outcome.
For example, a user has an explicit DENY that is associated with their IAM rule policy; that DENY overrides any ALLOW.
There are three ways to use a role:
Interactively in the IAM section of the AWS Management Console
Programmatically with the AWS CLI
Via the AWS SDKs (API calls)
An application or a service such as Amazon EC2 can assume a role by requesting temporary security credentials for a role that the service can use to make programmatic requests to AWS.

IAM roles also support single sign-on solutions. For example, an IAM administrator could configure SAML 2.0 federation instead of creating IAM users in an AWS account. With an identity provider, user identities can be managed outside of AWS, and these external user identities could be granted permissions to access resources in the AWS account.
For additional information see the following resources:
AWS Identity and Access Management: IAM Roles (Delegation and Federation): http://docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/id_roles.html
AWS Identity and Access Management: How Roles Differ from Resource-Based Policies: http://docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/id_roles_compare-resource-policies.html
AWS Identity and Access Management: Overview of IAM Policies: http://docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/access_policies.html

texts: Who has access to a particular resource?
What does a particular entity have access to?
notes: IAM users in the account can assume an IAM role to temporarily use the permissions of the role in the console. The user gives up their original permissions and takes on the permissions assigned to the role. When the user exits the role, their original permissions are restored. A user can switch roles to access resources in the AWS account, or even switch roles to access resources in other AWS accounts, which is called cross-account access.

Cross-account access grants access from another AWS account. This could be an account you own, or an account owned by another person. If the account is owned by another person or organization, it is a best practice to also provide a shared secret called an external ID. This stops one AWS account from guessing the role ARN for a different account and handing that to a common deputized AWS account. By configuring roles, an IAM administrator can grant the needed access without sharing the permanent AWS security credentials. For more information, see https://blogs.aws.amazon.com/security/post/Tx2Q5SSG3SFRRHO/How-to-Use-External-ID-When-Granting-Access-to-Your-AWS-Resources

A role has a permissions policy that defines what the role can do with these temporary security credentials. These permissions can specify AWS services and the respective actions, such as “CreateSubnet” in the Amazon VPC service. Additionally, conditions can be used to provide restrictions that can be based on time, date, source IP, and other factors.

AWS provides managed policies that can be attached to a role; whereas, inline policies can also be used where needed. The use of managed policies will usually make ongoing management easier. See the following for more information: http://docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/access_policies_managed-vs-inline.html

notes: Here are some best practices for IAM:

Avoid using the root account credentials for daily administration. Instead, when setting up a new account, define at least one new IAM user. Then, grant the user or users access so that most day-to-day tasks can be done using the IAM user credentials.

Delegate administration functions following the principle of least-privilege. Only grant access to services that are needed, and limit permissions within those services to only the parts needed. Additional rights can always be granted over time if the need arises.

Use IAM roles to provide cross-account access. Other best practices for IAM that were mentioned earlier in this module include configuring strong password policies, enabling MFA for any privileged users, and rotating credentials regularly. A full list of best practices for IAM can be found at https://docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/best-practices.html.
MFA is a good practice to implement for security purposes.

notes: There are three options for accessing AWS services. All three options are built on a common, REST-like API that serves as the foundation of AWS.

The AWS Management Console provides a rich graphical interface for a majority of the products and services offered by AWS. Occasionally, new features might not have all of their capabilities exposed through the console when the feature initially launches.
The AWS Command Line Interface (AWS CLI) provides a suite of utilities that can be run from a command program in Linux, MacOS, or Windows.

The software development kits (SDKs) are packages provided by AWS that enable access to AWS services using popular programming languages, such as Python, Ruby, .NET, or Java. The SDKs make it straightforward to use AWS in existing applications, and they also enable creating applications to deploy and monitor complex systems entirely via code.

The AWS CLI and the SDKs provide flexibility. They enable AWS users to create their own tools specific to their business and also to customize existing AWS features. For example, a user might create their own scripts or applications for launching Amazon EC2 instances that enforce using a specific set of AMIs, or add a standard set of tags to apply to resources that are created in the account.
The AWS CLI provides a programming language-agnostic way to automate and repeat the deployment of AWS resources, such as through Linux shell scripts or Windows batch files.

NOTE: All three modes of access can be used interchangeably. For example, an Amazon EC2 server created via an SDK call could be described using the appropriate command line call (aws ec2 describe-instances). This EC2 instance could later be terminated with a few clicks inside the AWS Management Console.
Note: Changes made via the AWS CLI or the API might take a few seconds or a few minutes to appear in the AWS Management Console.

texts: Available for Linux, Windows, and Mac
Use the aws configure command to specify defaults
notes: Here is a review of some basic information about the AWS CLI. The AWS CLI is available for use on Linux, Windows, and Mac platforms. It can also be installed on Linux and Windows EC2 instances, and it comes installed by default on Amazon Linux instances.

After installing the AWS CLI, the aws configure command can be used to set some defaults for all AWS CLI commands. The main defaults are the access key ID and the secret access key associated with the IAM account that you will use to access AWS resources. You can also specify a default Region for all commands.

The default output data format is a JSON document, which is best used in situations where the output will be handled programmatically. JSON is a de facto standard for data formatting and interchange on the internet that can be both easily read by humans, and it can be easily parsed by machines. Nearly all major programming languages and frameworks provide a way to convert JSON responses into objects or associative arrays.
However, there are also two other output formats that are supported by the AWS CLI:

ASCII-formatted table – The table output format is the most readable format because the data has human-readable representations within a tabular form. The command would be: $ export AWS_DEFAULT_OUTPUT="table"
Tab-delimited text – This text format displays data as text in tab-delimited lines, and it works well with Unix text processing tools, such as PowerShell scripts. The command would be: output=text
Additional information for controlling the command output when using the AWS CLI can be found at https://docs.aws.amazon.com/cli/latest/userguide/cli-usage-output.html.
The command-line format can be broken down into several parts. Each part specifies an action that will occur.
Use the aws command, which is the basic structure of an AWS command-line call. You are now ready to specify additional actions to occur.

Specify the top-level service to be called. For example, to invoke Amazon EC2, you would enter the command ec2, as shown in the diagram. A list of supported services can be found at http://docs.aws.amazon.com/cli/latest/reference/.

Specify the operation to be called. This is the operation that will be performed on the service specified in Step #2, such as stop-instances or run-instances. In the second example on the slide, the run-instances subcommand is being used to request the creation of a new Amazon EC2 instance.

Specify the parameters. One or more parameters can be specified depending on the operation that is called. Parameters are arguments or details that are used to perform the operation. Some operations have required parameters, while other operations do not require parameters. Most operations offer a few or many optional parameters as well. In the first example shown on the slide, the stop-instances operation requires an instance-id parameter (otherwise, it would be unclear which instance or instances should be stopped).

NOTE: Parameter names are preceded by two dashes (--). For example, to run the Amazon EC2 run-instances operation, several required parameters—and potentially some optional parameters—are specified. Required parameters include the AMI ID that is used to create the instance.
Lastly, specify the options. For example, after calling aws ec2 stop-instances use the --output option to specify the format of the response.

notes: The --query option can optionally be included in most commands to limit the results that are returned. Results are filtered on the client side.

You should format queries according to the JMESPath specification, which defines a syntax for searching JSON documents. For more information about JMESPath, see http://jmespath.org/specification.html.

Queries are constructed by designating the subsection of the response that you want to see. You can specify the subsection by addressing the full path to that section, starting from the top-most element of the response.

Array elements can be referenced using zero-based indexing. For example, to describe only the first instance returned by the Amazon EC2 describe-instances operation, use the path Reservations[0].Instances[0] in the query, which says: “For the first reservation, return the details about the first instance.” You could further specify that you want to see only specific attributes of this instance, such as its current operating state.

For another example, to view the states of all instances, you can use wildcards instead of indexes to return results from all reservations and all instances. The [*] syntax can be used in any array to specify that you want to view the specified property or child element for all members of that array.

Here’s a brief description of each of the commands shown on the slide and their respective actions:
Commands based on Amazon EC2:
aws ec2 run-instances: This command launches the specified number of instances from an AMI.
aws ec2 describe-instances: Describes any instances that exist in the account.
aws ec2 create-volume: Creates an Amazon EBS volume that can be attached to an instance in the same Availability Zone.
aws ec2 create-vpc: Creates a VPC with the Classless Inter-Domain Routing (CIDR) block specified.
Commands based on Amazon S3:

aws s3 ls: Lists Amazon S3 objects and common prefixes under a prefix or all Amazon S3 buckets. Optionally specify a specific bucket in the account, and the ls command will list the contents of the specified bucket.

aws s3 cp: Copies a file to, from, or between Amazon S3 locations. Use it to copy local files to Amazon S3, to copy a file from Amazon S3 to a laptop, or to copy Amazon S3 files to other Amazon S3 locations.
aws s3 mv: Moves a local file or Amazon S3 object to another location locally or in Amazon S3.
aws s3 rm: Deletes an Amazon S3 object.

notes: You are preparing to meet with your new customer, Mom & Pop Café & Bakery. The café is a new AWS customer and wants to explore using AWS services. You are now going to review the business introduction so you know more about your customer when determining a solution.
Let’s take a deeper look at our customer.

texts: My retirement dream became a reality…..
notes: The Mom & Pop Café & Bakery had its start from a retirement dream. The owners, Phillip and Emma, were not yet ready to sit around the house, and they wanted to do something that included their love of baking and supplemented their income. They love interacting with their local community and supporting military events across town with their baked goods and coffees.

Philip and Emma decided to open a café and bakery at the base of their flat in 2016. Their daughter, Sophie, and a secondary school student, Darsh, also work at the cafe. Since then, they have experienced an increase in local business and inquiries from people who travel through the area either for business or as a tourist.

texts: Mom & Pop Café & Bakery caters to:
notes: Mom & Pop Café & Bakery caters to different customers. Some customers are looking for an early breakfast and want to enjoy the atmosphere. Others need to hurry out with an order to go, whether they are busy workers who are part of the afternoon lunch traffic or London commuters. Some customers want to spend a lazy Saturday morning people-watching over a good espresso and conversation.

The interior of the café is unique. It has rustic, handmade wooden benches and tables finished with industrial elements. The ambience is softened by greenery, cozy lighting, and vintage signage from Phillip’s travels.
rendered: Mom & Pop Café & Bakery caters to:

texts: Often sells out 30 minutes after opening
notes: Phillip’s mother developed her recipes long ago. Her recipes are uniquely delicious, and they are also healthful. The recipes use simple ingredients and are based on seasonal availability. They have been carefully passed down and are a guarded secret.
The café is filled with the scent of globally sourced, fresh-ground coffee and the light, sweet aroma of Phillip’s cinnamon pastries. These pastries often disappear within 30 minutes after opening.

texts: Café customer purchases help two communities
notes: The café’s menu options are listed on a chalkboard that sits behind the counter. Baked goods are enticingly arranged in counter-based displays and a glass case. Café music plays softly, punctuated by the periodic sound of coffee grinding.

The chalkboard highlights a monthly changing menu of single-origin espressos made with beans that come directly from a coffee farm and are roasted in small batches. Phillip loves the idea that the farmer gets a financial benefit that also boosts their local economy. Café customers know that they are helping two communities with their purchase: their own community and the farmer’s community.
Phillip (pop) likes to bake and use his mother’s recipes. He is not a technology expert, so he tries to avoid computers.

He has traveled all over the world. his travel experiences led him to source some of the finest coffees from around the world, and many are ground fresh onsite. He has met many of the farmers who grow the beans he uses, and he has even met some farmers who grow some of the baking ingredients. He is interested in expanding the global presence of the café with the help of Sophie.

Owning a café is a good fit with his lifestyle, since he always woken up early, ever since he joined the Navy when he was 19. He is recently realizing however that he cannot do everything. His daughter Sophie reminds him of this every day. She says technology might be a benefit if he could learn more about it.
Emma (mom) is a retired accountant and she uses her skills for the café’s books. She knows how to use basic technology and she is really good with an Excel spreadsheet.

She does not mind helping Phillip in the kitchen, but she prefers to use her accounting skills to reinvest in the café. She want to enjoy more of her retirement, and she does not want to start a second career when she reaches retirement age.

While she enjoys working at the café, she would like to spend less time doing administrative tasks. She wants to head off to more yoga retreats with her best friend. Looking ahead, she wants time to enjoy being with her future grandchildren.

texts: Occupation: Cafe Manager and Future Business Student
notes: Sophie will be attending university next month to study Business. She currently runs the café and manages the supply orders and ingredient inventory. She also makes sure that deliveries across town are completed. Her customers call her the caffeine connoisseur.
She also likes programming. She took some programming classes in secondary school and thinks they would fit in well with a graduate degree in business.

Sophie just learned about Amazon Web Services and told her parents that their services could be used to automate the business. She knows that AWS services could help her parents focus more on what they want to do with the shop and reduce their administrative work.
She heard about AWS from one of her customers, Alejandro. He drops in daily for his usual cinnamon roll and handed her a business card in case she had any questions.

Darsh is completing secondary school in the spring. He has worked at the café for almost a year now. He is in charge of store upkeep and bicycle deliveries. He has been recently working behind the counter more, serving customers at Sophie’s direction. She told hime that because she is going to the university next month, it would be good for him to learn more about the café. He is eager to help out more.
Darsh likes art, and he wants to be a graphic artist after he completes school. He likes technology as well.
Now, let’s look at the AWS team that will be assisting the Mom & Pop Bakery & Café.

Alejandro is an AWS Technical Account Manager (TAM). He is also one of the café’s favorite customers, because he is there every day getting those delicious cinnamon rolls. He has to get there early, though, because they sell out quickly. He recently asked Sophie about the café’s website. He would like to help them expand their AWS presence and help their café do more, especially because they want to go global.

He gave his business card to Sophie so she could get in touch if she had any questions. He offered to meet with her and introduce her to the rest of my team so they could talk about the café’s business needs.

Raquel is an AWS Solutions Architect (SA) and she recently moved to London from Seattle. She used to be a network engineer and she has a strong background with advanced networking. She likes troubleshooting technical issues and creating frugal, resilient, and secure solutions for her customers.
It is a bonus that she also enjoys a good piece of cake when is designing a technical solution.
